d.title: Nobody implements h separate projections
d.caption: The equation says run attention `h` times on different learned projections, concatenate, and pass through `Wᴼ`. **In practice there is one `d_model × d_model` matrix per role, projected once and then *reshaped* into heads — mathematically identical and far faster**, because it is one large matrix multiply instead of `h` small ones. Which is worth knowing when reading an implementation: **the heads are a `view()` on a tensor, not a list of modules**, so there is nothing per-head to inspect except a slice.

nodes.label: The code: ONE d_model x d_model per role
Mathematically identical
nodes.sub: and one big matmul, not h small

nodes.label: So a head is a view(), not a module
W_O then mixes the concatenated heads

d.title: One head or sixty-four, the parameter count is identical
d.caption: **`d_k = d_model / h`, so the Q/K/V projections are always `d_model × d_model` in total — 262,144 each — and the count is 1,048,576 whatever `h` is.** Which is the reason multi-head attention was free to adopt: **more heads is not more capacity, it is the same capacity partitioned differently.** And it does cost something the table cannot show — **each head works in a `d_k`-dimensional subspace, so 64 heads means 8 dimensions per head**, which is too few to represent much.

d.title: Eight of twelve heads send most of their weight to [SEP]
d.caption: The claim under test is that head 1 learns syntax, head 2 semantics, head 3 proximity, head 4 coreference. **What layer 4 of `bert-base-uncased` actually does on a centre-embedded sentence: head 3 puts 0.7180 of its weight on `[SEP]` with an entropy of 0.7883, and most heads are in the same regime.** These are **attention sinks** — a head with nothing to contribute parks its mass on a token that carries no content. **The tidy division of labour is not what the weights show.**

d.title: One head, found by search, that reads the previous token
d.caption: **Searching all 144 heads for the highest average weight on the immediately preceding token found layer 3, head 5 at mean weight 0.7165** — and its per-token behaviour is clean: `on → sat` at 0.984, `sat → chased` at 0.941, `that → cat` at 0.967. **So genuinely interpretable heads do exist; they are found by searching rather than by reading a diagram.** The first two rows show the boundary condition — **the first content tokens have no previous token to read, so they fall back to `[CLS]`.**

d.title: The same head index behaves completely differently by depth
d.caption: Head 0 traced through all twelve layers: **mean offset goes from +0.93 to −2.07 to +6.50, entropy from 2.5284 down to 0.0220 at layer 2 and back up, and `[SEP]` weight from 0.0760 to 0.8644.** Compare that with the within-layer spread in §04 and the conclusion is clear: **depth changes a head's behaviour far more than head index does.** And the pairwise measurement makes the middle position precise — **mean cosine 0.7132 between heads in one layer, min 0.4511, max 0.9004: real diversity, no independence.**

d.title: Token 0 sees one position and token 4 sees five
d.caption: The mask is `tril(ones(n, n))` and the consequence is worth stating in terms of what each position gets: **token 0 has one input — itself — so its representation is a function of a single token, while token 4 has five.** Which means **the early positions of a sequence are intrinsically less informed than the later ones**, and it is why a decoder's first few tokens are the hardest to predict and why `[CLS]`-style prefix tokens become attention sinks (§4.4): position 0 has nowhere else to look.

d.title: Masking does not zero one weight — it redistributes all of them
d.caption: One row: *sat* attending to `[The, cat, sat, future]` with scaled scores `[0.40, 0.53, 0.59, 0.95]`. **Masked, the weights are `[0.2987, 0.3401, 0.3612, 0.0000]`; unmasked, they are `[0.1968, 0.2241, 0.2380, 0.3411]`.** So the three legitimate weights each **rose** when the future was masked — **the softmax renormalises over what is left, which is why masking is a change to the denominator rather than a filter on the output.** The reference's `[0.299, 0.340, 0.361, 0.000]` reproduces exactly.

steps.note: its mass went to the others

d.title: Minus ten leaks 4.49e-06 of exactly the information the mask exists to hide
d.caption: **In float32, anything below roughly `-1e4` underflows to exactly zero after the exponential, so `-inf` and `-1e9` are equivalent — both give a masked weight of 0.000e+00.** A merely *large* negative number does not: **`-10` leaves 4.492e-06 on a position the model must not see.** Small, and it is a leak of the future, **which makes the bug invisible in a loss curve and visible only as a model that is mysteriously good at next-token prediction.**

d.title: An identity, not an assumption — which is why the loss is what it is
d.caption: **Any joint distribution factorises as a product of conditionals; that is the chain rule, not a modelling choice.** So an autoregressive model is not approximating the joint distribution with an independence assumption — **it is learning each exact conditional, and maximising the sequence log-likelihood is *exactly* minimising next-token cross-entropy.** Which is why the training objective needs no justification beyond the factorisation: **`p("the cat sat") = p("the") · p("cat" | "the") · p("sat" | "the", "cat")`.**

nodes.label: So no independence assumption is made
Which is why the loss needs no argument
nodes.sub: it falls out of the factorisation

d.title: Mean 0.6488 under teacher forcing, and a minimum of 0.0836
d.caption: **Training always conditions on a correct prefix; inference conditions on whatever the model produced, mistakes included.** Scored with teacher forcing against a gold continuation GPT-2 would not have chosen, **the mean probability is 0.6488 and the minimum is 0.0836 at `' Italy'`** — the one token where the gold path diverges from the model's own preference. Left to generate, **it picks Berlin, then Washington, then London: a template it is confident in.** The gap between those two regimes is exposure bias.

d.title: Four families, and only one of them cannot generate at all
d.caption: The weaknesses are the content. **Autoregressive is the quality answer and costs `O(n)` sequential passes — which is 3.5's latency problem at its root.** Bidirectional MLM is an excellent encoder and **cannot generate**, because every position sees both sides. **Non-autoregressive emits every token in parallel and is weaker for a specific reason: it has no left context while deciding**, so it cannot condition on its own earlier choices. Diffusion LMs are improving fast and still behind.

state: left to right, one per step

d.title: Two thirds of the non-embedding parameters are in the part that cannot see other tokens
d.caption: **`512 → 2048 → 512` is 2,097,152 parameters per layer, about two thirds of all non-embedding parameters** — and it is applied **independently and identically to every position**, so it has no idea other tokens exist. That division of labour is the design: **attention *mixes* information between tokens, the FFN *transforms* each token on its own, and a block alternates between the two.** Which also explains why the FFN is where most of the model's stored knowledge is found: it is where most of the weights are.

nodes.label: The FFN TRANSFORMS each token alone
A block alternates between the two

d.title: GELU and SiLU go negative, and the tanh approximation is accurate to 4.13e-04
d.caption: **GELU weights the input by the probability that a standard normal falls below it — a smooth gate rather than ReLU's hard cutoff.** The rows worth reading are the negative ones: **GELU and SiLU dip negative for small negative inputs and return toward zero further out, so they do not hard-zero and the gradient never dies completely the way ReLU's does.** And the practical note: **max |exact − tanh approximation| is 4.13e-04**, so the cheap version is indistinguishable in practice.

d.title: The two-thirds rule balances the budget to four decimal places
d.caption: A gated linear unit **splits the up-projection into two branches and multiplies them elementwise, one acting as a learned gate — three weight matrices instead of two — so `d_ff` shrinks by two thirds to keep the budget fixed.** It is commonly stated as a rule of thumb; measured, it is near-exact: **2,096,640 against 2,097,152 at `d_model=512` (0.9998×), and 134,209,536 against 134,217,728 at 4096 (0.9999×).** So SwiGLU is a **free** substitution in parameter terms, which is why it displaced plain GELU FFNs.

d.title: Across the features, per token — which is why batch size 1 is safe
d.caption: **Normalisation runs across the feature dimension for each token, not across the batch** — and that independence from batch statistics is what makes it safe with variable sequence lengths and at batch size 1, **which BatchNorm is not.** The worked example reproduces exactly: **μ = 5, σ² = 4, σ = 2, and `x_hat = [-1.5, -0.5, -0.5, -0.5, 0, 0, 1.0, 2.0]` with mean 0 and variance 1.0000**, agreeing with `nn.LayerNorm` to four decimal places.

d.title: RMSNorm does not centre, and it was 161% slower here
d.caption: Same input: **mean of squares 29, RMS 5.3852, and an output whose mean is 0.9285 rather than 0** — because RMSNorm divides by the root mean square without subtracting the mean, so **it rescales without centring.** That is the whole simplification, and it is usually described as the faster option. **Measured on torch 2.10 CPU at `d=4096`: LayerNorm 43.80 ms against RMSNorm 114.32 ms — 161% slower, and `nn.RMSNorm` is no better.** The reason is implementation, not arithmetic: **LayerNorm has a fused ATen kernel and RMSNorm here does not.**
